stem: Scrum.org describes Product Backlog management as adjusting and ordering items so that the team can:
options: Finish all items in the agreed order
explanation: Product Backlog management is the act of adjusting and ordering items on the Product Backlog so the Scrum Team can deliver the most valuable product possible.

stem: Who defines the Sprint Goal during Sprint Planning?
explanation: After the Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value, the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal. The Product Owner brings a proposal, not a finished goal.

stem: Which Key Value Area measures the value a product delivers today?
explanation: Current Value quantifies the value the product delivers today. Unrealized Value looks at potential future value.

stem: What does a Product Vision describe?
options: Future state the team plans against
explanation: Scrum.org describes the Product Vision as the purpose of a product: the value it should deliver and to whom.

stem: What does Scrum encourage with stakeholders, and customers in particular?
options: A signed scope agreement up front
explanation: Scrum.org notes that Scrum encourages frequent collaboration with stakeholders, and customers in particular.

stem: According to Scrum.org, how should a product usually be delivered?
options: One launch once the core features are Done
Quarterly releases with full regression tests
At the end of each Sprint, after the Review
explanation: Scrum.org describes forecasting and release planning as a guide for delivering through small incremental and frequent releases rather than big bang launches.

stem: Besides value, what else may the Product Owner weigh when ordering items?
explanation: Ordering aims at value, but risk, dependencies between items and what the team needs to learn also shape which items come first.

stem: How are Product Backlog items chosen for the Sprint?
options: Product Owner selects them, and then the Developers confirm the fit
Whole Scrum Team votes, guided by the Scrum Master
Developers take the top items up to their past velocity
Developers select them, in discussion with the Product Owner
explanation: Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog for the current Sprint. The more the Developers know about their past performance and capacity, the more confident their forecast.

stem: A Product Owner tracks how far users' current experience falls short of what they want. Which Key Value Area is this?
explanation: The customer or user satisfaction gap, the difference between desired and current experience, is an example measure of Unrealized Value.

stem: Which two things does a good Product Vision express? (Choose two.)
explanation: A good Product Vision expresses the value the product should deliver and to whom that value is delivered. Technology, order and budgets are decided elsewhere and change more often.

stem: Why should the Product Owner learn the challenges key stakeholders face?
options: To deliver the value they are seeking
To agree their priorities in advance of work
To set the Sprint Goal on their behalf
explanation: Understanding the challenges stakeholders face helps the Scrum Team deliver the value they are looking for.

stem: In Scrum.org's Professional Scrum Competencies, Product Backlog Management is a focus area of which competency?
options: Understanding and Applying the Scrum Framework
explanation: Scrum.org lists Product Backlog Management under Managing Products with Agility, with Forecasting & Release Planning, Product Vision, Product Value, Business Strategy and Stakeholders & Customers.

stem: What is the main risk of a single big bang launch after a year of work?
options: Testing everything at once takes much longer
Marketing has less to announce later
Learning whether it works comes very late
explanation: Waiting a year to release delays all real feedback, so wrong assumptions are found late and are costly to fix.

stem: True or false: The Product Owner takes part in the Sprint Retrospective as a member of the Scrum Team.
explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is for the whole Scrum Team, and the Product Owner is part of the Scrum Team. Improvements in how the team works often depend on the Product Owner too.

stem: Release frequency belongs to which Key Value Area?
explanation: Time-to-Market measures how quickly the organization can deliver and learn from feedback. Release frequency, lead time and cycle time are examples.

stem: What does the Scrum Guide call the Product Backlog?
options: Prioritized list of approved product requirements
Emergent, ordered list of what the product needs
Concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal
Plan by and for the Developers for one Sprint
explanation: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product. It changes as the product and market change.

stem: How does business strategy relate to product visions?
options: Product visions add up to the strategy
Strategy and vision are owned separately
The vision is set by the Scrum Team, apart from strategy
explanation: Business strategy is informed by the company's mission and vision, and in turn informs individual product visions.

stem: What is the main reason to invite real customers to the Sprint Review?
options: They can add items to the next Sprint
They can see that progress is on plan
They can accept the Increment formally
Their feedback shapes what comes next
explanation: At the Sprint Review attendees inspect the Increment and collaborate on what to do next. Customer feedback is direct evidence for adapting the Product Backlog.

stem: The Product Owner orders the backlog from artifacts that are out of date. What does the Scrum Guide warn this can lead to?
options: Decisions that diminish value and increase risk
Forecasts that are far too cautious to be useful
Refinement that has to be repeated later
Sprint Goals that change during the Sprint
explanation: Scrum decisions are based on the perceived state of the artifacts. When transparency is low, those decisions can diminish value and increase risk.

stem: Technical debt is an example measure for which Key Value Area?
explanation: Ability to Innovate quantifies how effectively the organization delivers new capabilities. Technical debt, defect trends and innovation rate are listed examples.

stem: True or false: Defects and technical work belong in the Product Backlog alongside new features.
explanation: The Product Backlog is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team, so fixes and technical work are ordered there with everything else.

stem: True or false: The Scrum Guide defines a separate release planning event.
explanation: The Scrum Guide has five events and none of them is release planning. Teams may plan releases however they like, within Scrum.

stem: How should an organization adapt its business strategy?
options: At each annual strategic planning cycle
When a new product is approved
explanation: An organization inspects and adapts its business strategy based on feedback gathered from delivering product Increments, not only at fixed planning dates.

stem: Sales and support each say their item must come first. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Split the next Sprint between them
Ask both to agree on one order
Raise it with the sponsor to decide
Decide the order and explain why
explanation: The Product Owner represents many stakeholders and makes the ordering decision. Explaining it keeps the decision transparent and respected.

stem: A large item must be split. Which split usually serves the Product Owner best?
options: Thin slices, each usable on its own
Parts small enough for one Developer each
Steps of the workflow, such as design then build
Layers such as database, logic and screens
explanation: Slices that each create something usable can be released and inspected on their own. Splitting by layer or phase gives nothing usable until every part is Done.

stem: The Product Owner prepares attendees for Sprint Planning. Which two topics should they be ready to discuss? (Choose two.)
options: How those items map to the Product Goal
explanation: The Product Owner ensures attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal. The Developers plan their own work and capacity.

stem: The team doubled the number of features shipped, but customer satisfaction is flat. What does EBM suggest?
options: Track velocity instead; satisfaction is outside our control
More output has not improved outcomes
The survey method needs to change
Satisfaction lags and will rise again soon
explanation: The EBM Guide notes that more features (outputs) do not necessarily lead to improved customer experiences (outcomes). Value is judged by outcomes.

stem: Stakeholders want to know how much of the backlog will be Done by a date. What is the best basis for the forecast?
options: Capacity the team plans to have
Plan agreed with stakeholders at the start
Progress the team has actually achieved
explanation: Forecasts are most reliable when based on what has already happened, such as actual delivered progress. Hopes and capacity claims are not evidence.

stem: Who may suggest new Product Backlog items?
options: Product Owner and Developers, in refinement
Scrum Team members, but not stakeholders
Anyone; the Product Owner orders them
explanation: Ideas can come from anyone, but the Product Owner remains accountable for the Product Backlog and its order. Others change it by convincing the Product Owner.

stem: The Product Goal is met two Sprints early. What should the Product Owner do next?
options: Set and share the next Product Goal
Use the spare Sprints to refine the backlog
Keep the goal and add stretch items to it
Close the product and release the team
explanation: Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal is part of the Product Owner's accountability. Once one is fulfilled, the team needs a new target to plan against.

stem: True or false: Developers may talk with users directly to understand a Product Backlog item.
explanation: The whole Scrum Team is responsible for stakeholder collaboration. Developers talking with users helps them understand items, while the Product Owner still owns the order.

stem: Besides the work done in the Sprint, what progress is discussed at the Sprint Review?
explanation: At the Sprint Review the Scrum Team presents the results of its work, and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed with stakeholders.

stem: Which is an outcome rather than an output?
options: A new, faster checkout flow is released
explanation: Outcomes are things a customer or user experiences, such as staying with the product. Screens, items and velocity measure output or activity.

stem: How much time does the Scrum Guide set aside for Product Backlog refinement?
explanation: The Scrum Guide describes refinement as an ongoing activity and sets no timebox or percentage for it. The Scrum Team decides how much it needs.

stem: Why should a release forecast be updated each Sprint?
options: New evidence makes it more realistic
Scrum requires a forecast at each Review
Velocity must be recalculated by rule
explanation: Each Sprint adds real data on progress and on what is still needed. Updating the forecast keeps stakeholder expectations realistic.

stem: According to the Scrum Guide, what is a product?
options: Concrete stepping stone to a goal
explanation: The Scrum Guide calls a product a vehicle to deliver value, with a clear boundary, known stakeholders and well-defined users or customers.

stem: Who usually counts as a stakeholder of a product?
options: People who fund or sponsor the product
Users who interact with the product
Anyone with an interest in its outcome
Managers of the people who build it
explanation: Stakeholders include users, customers, sponsors, support staff and others with an interest in the product's outcome. A product has known stakeholders.

stem: True or false: The Scrum Guide requires the Product Owner to formally accept each item at the Sprint Review.
explanation: The Scrum Guide has no formal acceptance step. An item is part of the Increment once it meets the Definition of Done, and the Sprint Review is a working session, not a sign-off.

stem: True or false: Higher velocity shows that the product is delivering more value.
explanation: Velocity counts output, not value. Value shows up in outcomes for customers and the organization, such as satisfaction, usage and revenue.

stem: Which two attributes does refinement add to Product Backlog items? (Choose two.)
explanation: Refinement breaks items down and adds detail such as a description, order and size. Attributes often vary with the domain of work.

stem: Which focus area does Scrum.org list beside Product Backlog Management in the same competency?
explanation: Managing Products with Agility covers Forecasting & Release Planning, Product Vision, Product Value, Product Backlog Management, Business Strategy and Stakeholders & Customers. Self-Managing Teams, Empiricism and Scrum Values sit in other competencies.

stem: Usage data from the last release shows a new feature is rarely used. What is the best next step for the Product Owner?
options: Inspect why, then adapt the Product Backlog
Remove the feature in the next release
Wait one more release for clearer data
Discuss it at the next Sprint Retrospective
explanation: Empiricism means making decisions on what is observed. The Product Owner inspects the evidence and adapts the Product Backlog rather than following a plan that the data no longer supports.

stem: According to Scrum.org, what is the objective of a Scrum Team?
options: Meet the Sprint Goal every Sprint
Deliver value to customers and stakeholders
Deliver the agreed scope at a high quality
explanation: Scrum.org states that the objective of a Scrum Team is to deliver value to customers and stakeholders.

stem: True or false: In Scrum, a product can be a service, a physical product or something more abstract.
explanation: The Scrum Guide says a product could be a service, a physical product or something more abstract, as long as it delivers value.

stem: A sponsor asks for a feature the Product Owner thinks adds little value. What is the best response?
options: Add it near the top to keep the sponsor
Let the Sprint Review attendees decide
Share the evidence; keep it low or out
Build a small version to keep goodwill
explanation: Maximizing value sometimes means saying no. The Product Owner explains the reasoning with evidence and keeps the decision, which the organization must respect.

stem: A release date is fixed by law. What can the Product Owner adjust to meet it?
options: Sprint length, to fit more work in
Definition of Done, for this release only
Team size, adding people near the end
Scope, keeping the most valuable items
explanation: When the date cannot move, scope is the lever. Ordering by value means the most important items are Done by the date, without lowering quality.

stem: The Product Backlog has grown to thousands of items. What problem is most likely?
options: Transparency is lost; ordering gets hard
Product Goal gets harder to change
Refinement takes much more Sprint capacity
explanation: A huge backlog hides what matters and is hard to keep ordered and understood. Removing items that no longer serve the Product Goal restores transparency.

stem: Sprints enable predictability by inspecting and adapting progress toward the Product Goal at least how often?
explanation: Because a Sprint lasts one month or less, progress toward the Product Goal is inspected and adapted at least every calendar month.

stem: Scrum.org says product value drives which two of these? (Choose two.)
explanation: Product value drives customer satisfaction, loyalty, brand reputation and the longevity of a business by meeting customers' needs.

stem: In Evidence-Based Management, which goal is the organization's current improvement focus?
explanation: Immediate Tactical Goals are the current focus of improvement. Intermediate Goals mark the path, and Strategic Goals are the large, distant outcomes.

stem: Which two happen with stakeholders at a Sprint Review? (Choose two.)
explanation: Attendees inspect the outcome of the Sprint and collaborate on what to do next. Tasks, hours and individual ratings are not part of it.

stem: True or false: A Product Backlog is complete once the first release ships.
explanation: The Product Backlog is emergent. It changes as long as the product exists and keeps changing as the team and stakeholders learn.

stem: When can the Product Owner release an Increment?
options: When the Developers say it is stable
At the end of the Sprint, after the Review
Once a planned release is complete
Whenever it is Done and worth releasing
explanation: An Increment that meets the Definition of Done can be released whenever it creates value; releases are not tied to the end of a Sprint.

stem: Who decides how much work the Developers take into the Sprint?
explanation: Selecting how much can be completed in a Sprint may be challenging, but it is the Developers' call, informed by their past performance, capacity and Definition of Done. The Product Owner influences what, not how much.

stem: Revenue per employee is an example measure of:
explanation: Revenue per employee, product cost ratio and customer and employee satisfaction are listed as Current Value measures.

stem: Who takes part in Product Backlog refinement?
options: Product Owner, with the Scrum Master
Product Owner and Developers, as needed
Developers, with the Scrum Master leading
explanation: Refinement is a collaborative activity. The Product Owner brings the needs and value, and the Developers who will do the work size the items.

stem: Why are Strategic Goals in Evidence-Based Management pursued empirically?
options: They depend on the Developers' estimates
They are made of many Sprint Goals
They are reviewed by leaders each year
They are large, distant and uncertain
explanation: Strategic Goals are so large and far away, with so many uncertainties, that the path to them can only be found through empiricism.

stem: The Product Owner struggles to get two departments to work together on the product. Who can help facilitate?
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the Product Owner by facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed, and removes barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

stem: True or false: Product Backlog refinement is one of the five Scrum events.
explanation: The Scrum events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. Refinement is an ongoing activity, not an event.

stem: Which pair of Key Value Areas reflects the organization's capability to deliver value?
options: Unrealized Value and Ability to Innovate
explanation: Current and Unrealized Value reflect customer outcomes in the market. Time-to-Market and Ability to Innovate reflect the organization's ability to deliver them.

stem: A stakeholder asks to see why an item sits low in the Product Backlog. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Move it up a little as a goodwill gesture
Refer them to the sponsor who set the priorities
Walk them through how the order was set
Invite them to the next Sprint Planning
explanation: The Product Owner owns the order and keeps it transparent and understood. Explaining the reasoning keeps trust while the decision stays with the Product Owner.

stem: Which chart shows both completed work and changes in total scope over time?
explanation: A burn-up chart plots work completed against a separate total-scope line, so scope growth is visible. A simple burn-down shows remaining work only.

stem: Many teams argue over what the product is for. Which step helps the Product Owner most?
options: Set one Sprint Goal for all
explanation: A shared Product Vision gives everyone the same purpose to decide against, which reduces conflicting directions.

stem: Stakeholders keep being surprised by what is delivered. What would help most?
options: Inviting them to inspect each Increment
Sending them a detailed weekly status report
explanation: Frequent inspection at the Sprint Review keeps stakeholders' expectations in line with the real product and gives them a say in what comes next.

stem: Which two help Developers understand what a Product Backlog item needs? (Choose two.)
explanation: Clear items come from collaboration and concrete examples. Scrum does not require fixed hour estimates or stakeholder sign-off before work.

stem: A feature passes testing but misses one Definition of Done criterion on the last Sprint day. The Product Owner wants it in the Increment. What is correct?
options: It joins the Increment with a defect logged
It counts if the Product Owner accepts it
It is not part of the Increment yet
It is shown at the Review as nearly Done
explanation: Work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done. The Product Owner cannot waive the Definition of Done to count more work.

stem: What does the Innovation Rate measure?
options: Share of time teams spend on product work
Usage of each feature by customers
Share of effort spent on new capabilities
explanation: Innovation Rate is the percentage of effort or cost spent on new product capabilities, divided by total product effort or cost.

stem: True or false: A forecast in Scrum is a commitment that the stated scope will ship on the stated date.
explanation: A forecast is a best estimate from evidence so far. In complex work what will happen is unknown, so forecasts guide decisions rather than guarantee them.

stem: Why split large items before Sprint Planning?
options: So each can be Done within one Sprint
So each Developer can own an item
So each one can be estimated in hours
So the Sprint Backlog has more items
explanation: Items that can be Done within one Sprint are ready for selection. Large items are split so they fit and still deliver something usable.

stem: The Product Owner weighs three candidate Product Goals. What should guide the choice?
options: Which goal has the clearest business case
Which goal best serves the vision and strategy
Which goal the team can forecast best
explanation: Business strategy informs the Product Vision, and the Product Goal is the next target the team plans against. Choosing it against vision and strategy keeps the work pointed at value.

stem: Whose needs may the Product Owner represent in the Product Backlog?
explanation: The Scrum Guide says the Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog.

stem: Three Scrum Teams build one product. How many Product Goals do they work toward?
options: One per team, linked to an overall goal
explanation: Scrum Teams working on the same product share one Product Goal, one Product Backlog and one Product Owner.

stem: Item A helps most users a little; item B helps a few key customers a lot. Both cost the same. How should the Product Owner decide?
options: Compare evidence of each item's total value
Favour item A, since it reaches more users
Favour item B, since key customers pay most
Let the Developers pick the one easier to build
explanation: Neither reach nor customer importance settles value on its own. The Product Owner compares the evidence of total value for each item, then checks the result empirically after release.

stem: What is the single source of work for the Scrum Team?
explanation: The Scrum Guide calls the Product Backlog the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.

stem: Why release a small first version to real users early?
options: To reduce the cost of the final launch
To give marketing something to announce
To learn what users value before building more
To meet stakeholders' first agreed milestone date
explanation: An early release turns assumptions into evidence. The Product Owner can then order the rest of the backlog on what users actually do.

stem: In Evidence-Based Management, what is a hypothesis?
options: Measure chosen to track one Key Value Area
Test designed to prove or reject a belief
Belief that one change will lead to a result
explanation: The EBM Guide defines a hypothesis as a belief that doing something will lead to something else. It stays a belief until an experiment supports or rejects it.

stem: True or false: Users and customers are always the same people.
explanation: A customer may pay while others use the product, as in a company buying software for its staff. The Product Owner considers both.

stem: The Product Owner sees technical debt slowing every release. What should they do?
options: Raise it with the Developers and weigh it
Set aside a fixed share of each Sprint
Leave it for the Developers to fit in later
Make removing it the next Sprint Goal
explanation: Technical debt reduces the ability to deliver value, so the Product Owner makes it transparent and weighs the work against other items. How the code is fixed stays with the Developers.

stem: True or false: Evidence-Based Management prescribes one fixed set of Key Value Measures for every organization.
explanation: EBM defines no specific Key Value Measures, so organizations can adapt them. The measures in the guide are examples.

stem: The Product Owner orders items only by which stakeholder is most senior. What is the main risk?
options: Value is not maximized for customers
explanation: Ordering by rank rather than by value, risk and learning means the most valuable work may wait. The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value.

stem: What is the main purpose of ordering the Product Backlog?
options: Show the team its next Sprint Goal
Make the most valuable work come first
explanation: Ordering puts the work that maximizes value, given risk and dependencies, at the top so the team takes it on first.

stem: Which event is the main chance for the Product Owner and stakeholders to inspect the Increment together?
explanation: The Sprint Review is where the Scrum Team presents its results to key stakeholders and they inspect the outcome of the Sprint together.

stem: Which Key Value Area looks at value the product could create but does not yet?
explanation: Unrealized Value measures potential future value that could be realized if the organization better met the needs of all potential customers or users.

stem: What informs a company's business strategy?
explanation: Business strategy is informed by the company's mission and vision, then informs the visions of individual products.

stem: A stakeholder group is affected by the product but has never been asked for input. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Ask the sponsor to speak for them
Invite them to the Daily Scrum
Find ways to learn their needs
Represent them using existing user data
explanation: Identifying and learning about key stakeholders' challenges helps the Scrum Team deliver value. A missing group is a blind spot.

stem: Whose accountability covers judging whether releasing a Done Increment now maximizes value?
explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value, so judging when releasing an Increment creates value sits with them.

stem: Which of these belongs in the Product Backlog?
options: Work approved by the steering group
Features and fixes; tech work stays apart
explanation: The Product Backlog lists what is needed to improve the product: features, fixes, technical work and experiments alike.

stem: In Sprint Planning, the Product Owner's main contribution to 'what can be Done' is:
options: Decide how many items fit in the Sprint
Clarify items so Developers can choose
Confirm the Sprint Backlog is complete
Agree the task breakdown with Developers
explanation: The Product Owner helps the Developers understand the items so they can select and forecast. How much fits and how the work is done remain the Developers' decisions.

stem: Lead time belongs to which Key Value Area?
explanation: Lead time, release frequency and customer cycle time all describe how quickly the organization delivers and learns, so they are Time-to-Market measures.

stem: In Evidence-Based Management, what shows the organization is on the path to a Strategic Goal?
explanation: Intermediate Goals are achievements that show the organization is on the path toward a Strategic Goal, where the path is somewhat uncertain but not completely unknown.

stem: Stakeholders want the Product Owner to give every department equal Sprint time. What is the weakness?
options: It ignores where value is highest
It makes Sprint Planning slower to run
It leaves no capacity for technical debt
explanation: Sharing time by department ignores where the most value lies. The Product Owner orders by value so the team works on what matters most.

stem: Items at the bottom of the backlog have one-line descriptions. Is this a problem?
options: Yes; each needs acceptance criteria first
No; detail is added as they near the top
Yes; vague items hide their real size
No, as long as they are estimated
explanation: Refinement adds detail as items approach selection. Detailing distant items early wastes effort, since many will change or be removed.

stem: Over five Sprints a team completed 18, 22, 20, 19 and 21 points. Which forecast is most useful?
options: Exactly 22, the team's best so far
A range, about 18 to 22 next Sprint
explanation: Past results suggest a range around 20 per Sprint. A range shows uncertainty honestly; a stretch number or a fixed maximum ignores the evidence.

stem: True or false: The Scrum Team may invite people from outside the team to Sprint Planning to give advice.
explanation: The Scrum Guide allows the Scrum Team to invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice, for example a specialist or a customer representative.

stem: The number of product versions still being supported is a measure of:
explanation: The Installed Version Index counts the versions still supported. Supporting many versions drains capacity for new capabilities, so it is an Ability to Innovate measure.

stem: True or false: Removing items from the Product Backlog that no longer serve the Product Goal is part of managing it well.
explanation: Product Backlog management includes adjusting the backlog. Dropping items that no longer serve the Product Goal keeps it transparent and focused.

stem: According to the EBM Guide, what are Mission and Vision without goals?
explanation: The EBM Guide says that without goals, the Mission and Vision are simply lofty aspirations. Goals make progress toward them measurable.

stem: A key customer is unhappy with the latest Increment. What should the Product Owner do first?
options: Fix the issues in the current Sprint
Find out why, then adapt the backlog
Put their complaints at the top of the backlog
Raise it at the next Daily Scrum
explanation: Customer dissatisfaction is evidence. Understanding its cause lets the Product Owner adapt the Product Backlog where it adds the most value.

stem: Why should the Product Owner prefer to release small Increments often?
options: Smaller releases need less testing and less sign-off
Small releases make velocity more stable
Each release brings feedback to inspect and adapt on
explanation: Each Increment delivered to users creates evidence. Releasing often gives the Product Owner more chances to inspect real outcomes and adapt the Product Backlog.

stem: Potential market share is an example measure of:
explanation: Potential market share describes value not yet captured, so it is listed under Unrealized Value.

stem: A business analyst writes most Product Backlog items. What is still the Product Owner's job?
options: Ordering the items and owning the outcome
Reviewing each item that the analyst writes
Presenting the items at Sprint Planning
explanation: The Product Owner may have others do Product Backlog work, but ordering and accountability for value remain with the Product Owner.

stem: A sponsor wants every backlog item by a fixed date. What should the Product Owner explain?
options: A detailed plan will make it certain
Scope or date may have to change
The team can commit if it adds people
A buffer can absorb most of the risk
explanation: In complex work the future is uncertain. Forecasts show what is likely, and either scope or date may need to change; lowering quality is not an option.

stem: A new law makes the current Product Goal pointless. What is the most fitting action?
options: Finish it first, then set the next goal
Cancel the Sprint and keep the goal
Abandon it and set a new Product Goal
Reword it to fit the new law
explanation: A Product Goal must be fulfilled or abandoned before the next one is taken on. When it no longer makes sense, the Product Owner can abandon it and develop a new one.

stem: The Product Owner is the only person who ever speaks with users. What is the main risk?
options: The Product Owner becomes badly overloaded
Developers lose direct insight into needs
explanation: The whole Scrum Team is responsible for stakeholder collaboration. When only one person talks to users, the Developers build with less understanding of the need.

stem: A new item could validate whether a whole feature area is worth building. Why might it be ordered high?
options: It brings learning that guides later ordering
It is a learning task for new Developers
It makes the Sprint Goal easier to set
It keeps key stakeholders engaged early on
explanation: Items that create learning reduce uncertainty about the value of later work, so the Product Owner can order the rest with better evidence.

stem: Mid-Sprint, the Product Owner has a valuable new idea that does not fit the Sprint Goal. Where does it go?
options: Into the Sprint Backlog if the Developers all agree
Into the Product Backlog, ordered for a later Sprint
Into the next Sprint Goal, so it is not lost
Into a parking list until the Sprint Review
explanation: Work that does not serve the current Sprint Goal is added to the Product Backlog, where the Product Owner orders it against everything else for future Sprints.

stem: What does the Customer Usage Index help a Product Owner infer?
options: How much of the market is still untapped
How often customers return each week
How useful customers find each feature
How large the gap in customer satisfaction is
explanation: The Customer Usage Index measures usage by feature to help infer how useful customers find the product. It is a Current Value measure.

stem: Which measure best shows how often value reaches users?
explanation: Release frequency is a Time-to-Market measure in Evidence-Based Management. Velocity and backlog size do not show whether value reached users.

stem: An online shop item reads 'Customers can pay'. Which first slice delivers usable value soonest?
options: Pay by one common card type
explanation: A thin slice, one payment method working end to end, can be released and tested with real customers. The others deliver nothing usable on their own.

stem: Which two describe a product in the Scrum Guide? (Choose two.)
explanation: A product has a clear boundary, known stakeholders and well-defined users or customers. Budgets and end dates are not part of the definition.

stem: Who brings the stakeholders' interests into the Product Backlog?
explanation: The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog and is accountable for its content and order.

stem: Which two artifacts does the Product Owner use to make product progress visible to stakeholders? (Choose two.)
explanation: The Product Backlog and the Increment are Scrum artifacts. The Product Owner's decisions are visible in the content and order of the Product Backlog and through the inspectable Increment.

stem: What does Time-to-Learn cover?
options: Start of release work to actual release
Idea to learning from users' use of it
explanation: Time-to-Learn is the total time to sketch an idea, build it, deliver it to users and learn from their usage.

stem: Which two are good reasons to remove an item from the Product Backlog? (Choose two.)
options: Its estimate is larger than a Sprint
Evidence shows users do not need it
It no longer serves the Product Goal
It has no acceptance criteria yet
Its requester has left the company
explanation: Removing items that no longer serve the Product Goal or that evidence shows are not needed keeps the backlog focused. Difficulty, author and a short wait are not reasons on their own.

stem: True or false: Time-to-Market measures how quickly an organization can deliver and learn from feedback.
explanation: In Evidence-Based Management, Time-to-Market quantifies how quickly the organization can deliver and learn from the feedback its experiments produce.

stem: Who is best placed to keep the Product Vision alive for the Scrum Team?
explanation: The Product Vision is a Scrum.org focus area rather than a Scrum Guide term. Because the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value and for developing and communicating the Product Goal, keeping the vision clear and shared sits with them.

stem: True or false: For the Product Owner to succeed, the whole organization must respect their decisions.
explanation: The Scrum Guide states that for Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions.

stem: True or false: All the work needed to reach the Product Goal happens within Sprints.
explanation: The Scrum Guide says all the work necessary to achieve the Product Goal happens within Sprints. There is no separate phase before or after them.

stem: A sponsor wants the Product Owner judged on items completed per Sprint. What is the main weakness?
options: It counts output, not customer outcomes
Item sizes differ far too much to compare
It ignores the quality of the items
It can be gamed by splitting items
explanation: Items completed is an output measure. EBM points out that output is easier to measure than outcomes, but more output does not necessarily mean more value.

stem: In Sprint Planning, the Developers keep finding the top items unclear. What does this suggest?
options: Sprint Planning needs a longer timebox
The Scrum Master should clarify items
Product Owner should write longer items
explanation: Refinement prepares items so they can be understood and selected. Repeatedly unclear items mean the Product Owner and Developers need to refine more before planning.

stem: True or false: Each Scrum Team on a single product should keep its own separate Product Backlog.
explanation: Scrum Teams on the same product share one Product Backlog, one Product Goal and one Product Owner.

stem: What is the most reliable evidence of progress toward the Product Goal?
explanation: Only work that meets the Definition of Done is part of an Increment, and each Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Effort and estimates are not progress.

stem: True or false: Outputs are easier to measure than outcomes.
explanation: The EBM Guide notes that activities and outputs are easier to measure than outcomes, which is one reason organizations fall back on them.

stem: True or false: Once set, a business strategy should stay fixed so teams are not distracted.
explanation: An organization inspects and adapts its business strategy using feedback from delivered Increments. Strategy is revisited as evidence arrives.

stem: Which source of feedback is usually strongest for the Product Owner?
options: What the Product Owner believes users want
What a competitor has just launched
explanation: Behaviour of real users with a released Increment is evidence. Beliefs and preferences are assumptions until validated by customers.

stem: Time to pivot is an example measure of which Key Value Area?
explanation: Time to pivot, like time-to-learn and release frequency, shows how fast the organization can change course and learn, so the EBM Guide lists it under Time-to-Market.

stem: A competitor launches a feature customers now expect. What can the Product Owner do right away?
options: Raise it at the next Sprint Review
Plan it into the next release
Add it to the current Sprint
explanation: The Product Owner can reorder the Product Backlog at any time to respond to change. Changing the current Sprint is only possible if it does not endanger the Sprint Goal.

stem: Which situation shows the Product Owner using adaptation well?
options: Reviewing the Product Goal every quarter
Keeping the roadmap stable so teams can plan
Reordering the backlog after users reject a new flow
Adding detail to all items before each Sprint Planning
explanation: Adaptation means adjusting as soon as an inspection shows something is unacceptable. Changing the Product Backlog in response to user feedback is adaptation in action.

stem: Which is the best sign that a new feature created value?
options: It was delivered on the planned date
Stakeholders praised it at the Review
Customers use it and stay longer
explanation: Value shows up in customer outcomes such as usage and retention. Delivery dates, points and team enjoyment describe the work, not its value.

stem: Which statement best fits a Product Goal?
options: Make online booking the way most patients reach us
Release the whole new booking system by the end of June
Replace the booking database with a faster one
Add booking reminders, cancellations and payments
explanation: A Product Goal describes a future state of the product to plan against. A list of screens, a technical task or a count of Sprints is output, not a target state.

stem: A powerful executive demands a feature that conflicts with the Product Goal. What is the Product Owner's best first step?
options: Put it to a stakeholder vote at the Review
Explain the trade-off against the goal
Change the Product Goal to include it
Add it, since the executive funds the work
explanation: The Product Owner explains the trade-off against the Product Goal and value. The decision stays with the Product Owner, and the organization must respect it.

stem: Does Scrum require acceptance criteria on every Product Backlog item?
options: Yes; the Definition of Done needs them
Yes; they are part of being ready
Only for items near the top
explanation: Scrum does not prescribe acceptance criteria. Many teams use them as a complementary practice to make items clear.

stem: What is the purpose of release planning for a Scrum Team?
options: Plan of Increments for each Sprint
explanation: Scrum.org describes forecasting and release planning as a guide for delivering through small, frequent releases. It does not replace Sprint Planning or fix the future.

stem: How does a clear Sprint Goal help the Product Owner?
options: It keeps the Sprint focused on one valuable objective
It fixes the full scope the Developers will deliver
It sets the target for the next Product Goal
It tells stakeholders exactly what will be released
explanation: The Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint. It creates coherence and focus while leaving the Developers flexibility in the exact work needed.

stem: Which two are example measures of Ability to Innovate? (Choose two.)
explanation: Defect trends and the on-product index are listed under Ability to Innovate. Release frequency is Time-to-Market, revenue per employee is Current Value and potential market share is Unrealized Value.

stem: How should the Product Owner make the Product Backlog transparent?
options: Show the top items at each Sprint Review
Keep it visible and understood by all
Let the Scrum Master publish it weekly
Share a summary with stakeholders monthly
explanation: The Product Owner ensures the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood, so everyone inspects the same picture.

stem: In Evidence-Based Management, what is an experiment?
options: Measure chosen to track one Key Value Area
Belief that a change will lead to a result
Test designed to prove or reject a hypothesis
Small release made to gather opinions
explanation: The EBM Guide defines an experiment as a test designed to prove or reject a hypothesis.

stem: Which question best helps a Product Owner understand a customer's need?
options: Which competitor features should we copy?
When exactly do you need it delivered?
Which features do you want first?
What problem are you trying to solve?
explanation: Asking about the customer's problem uncovers the need behind a request. Solutions can then be chosen to deliver the value they seek.

stem: Which two statements about Scrum and complex product work are true? (Choose two.)
options: Forecasts become exact after a few Sprints
More is unknown than known at the start
Decisions should rest on what is observed
Detailed early analysis removes most risk
explanation: In complex work much is unknown, so Scrum relies on empiricism: decisions based on what is observed, with frequent inspection and adaptation.

stem: A feature has high value but huge cost; a smaller one gives most of the value at a tenth of the cost. What should the Product Owner weigh?
options: Total value delivered, whatever the cost
explanation: Ordering to maximize value means weighing the likely value of an item against its cost and risk. The cheaper item may return value sooner.

stem: Two items have similar value; one is much riskier. When is it wise to do the riskier one first?
options: When it needs the least refinement
When early failure would be cheaper to learn
When the Sprint is long enough to absorb all of it
When the riskier item has a firm deadline
explanation: Doing risky work early exposes problems while they are cheap to fix and before other work depends on it.

stem: In a complex environment, what does the Scrum Guide say about future events?
options: Risks can be listed in advance
Only near-term events can be known
Most of it can be planned for
explanation: The Scrum Guide says that in complex environments what will happen is unknown, which is why forecasts rest on what has already happened.

stem: In the EBM empirical loop, what comes right after forming a hypothesis?
explanation: The loop is: set goals, form a hypothesis, run the experiment, inspect the results, then adapt. Inspection needs data from the experiment first.

stem: Which two are ways the Scrum Master supports stakeholder relations? (Choose two.)
options: Removing barriers between stakeholders and teams
Ordering requests for the Product Owner
Collecting stakeholder requests for the team
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organization by removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams and serves the Product Owner by facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed.

stem: Refinement shows an item is no longer needed. Who decides to remove it?
explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog's content and order, so removing an item is the Product Owner's decision, informed by others.

stem: The Product Owner keeps a private list of top priorities apart from the Product Backlog. Which pillar suffers most?
explanation: The Product Backlog is the single source of work and must be visible and understood. A hidden list means the team and stakeholders inspect a false picture.

stem: Employee satisfaction is listed under which Key Value Area?
explanation: Current Value asks how happy users, customers, employees and investors are today, so employee satisfaction is a Current Value measure.

stem: An Increment is Done, but marketing wants to wait three months to launch it with others. What should the Product Owner weigh?
options: How to keep the Increment's code stable
Whether the Developers can start the next item
Whether to re-test it before the launch
Value and learning lost by waiting
explanation: Holding Done work back delays value and feedback. The Product Owner weighs that against the benefits of a combined launch.

stem: What does a well-ordered Product Backlog give the Developers?
options: Clear view of what matters most next
Exact items for the next Sprint
Sprint Goal for the coming Sprint
Set order the Developers must follow item by item
explanation: An ordered Product Backlog shows the team what is most valuable to work on next, which makes Sprint Planning faster and more focused.

stem: True or false: In Evidence-Based Management, goals should be measurable and transparent.
explanation: EBM asks for measurable goals so progress can be judged, made transparent to the people working toward them.

stem: How does the Product Owner keep stakeholders informed between Sprint Reviews?
explanation: A transparent Product Backlog shows what is coming and why. The Daily Scrum is the Developers' event, not a stakeholder meeting.

stem: The Developers say an item is too large to finish in one Sprint. What should happen?
options: Give it to two Developers at the same time
Split it into smaller usable items
Take it in and extend the Sprint
explanation: Items that can be Done within one Sprint are ready for selection. Large items are broken down through refinement, with the Product Owner keeping the value in view.

stem: Mean time to repair is listed under which Key Value Area?
explanation: Mean time to repair, like lead time and deployment frequency, shows how quickly the organization can deliver and respond, so it is a Time-to-Market measure.

stem: A Developer suggests splitting an item into front end and back end parts. What should the Product Owner raise?
options: Neither part alone would be usable
Back end first reduces the most risk
Front end first shows progress sooner
Each part needs its own acceptance criteria
explanation: Splitting by technical layer often leaves pieces that cannot be released or inspected on their own. Slicing through all layers keeps each piece usable.

stem: What does a burn-down chart show?
explanation: A burn-down chart plots the work remaining against time. It is one of the forecasting practices the Scrum Guide mentions, but it is not required.

stem: Why does Evidence-Based Management pursue large goals in small steps?
options: Small steps are much easier to estimate and plan
Small steps fit inside one Sprint
Each step gives feedback on the direction
explanation: The EBM Guide says organizations must work toward larger goals in small steps, experimenting and learning along the way, because the path is uncertain.

stem: Which statement about stakeholders fits Scrum?
options: Only the Product Owner may speak with them
They attend the Daily Scrum to stay informed
Whole Scrum Team collaborates with them
explanation: The Scrum Team is responsible for stakeholder collaboration, so Developers and the Scrum Master work with stakeholders too. The Daily Scrum is for the Developers, and gathering requirements is not the Scrum Master's job.

stem: True or false: One Product Owner can be accountable for a product built by several Scrum Teams.
explanation: When several Scrum Teams work on the same product they share one Product Owner, along with one Product Goal and one Product Backlog.

stem: Which question belongs to Unrealized Value?
options: Is it worth pursuing untapped markets?
How fast can we adapt to new information?
What prevents customers using new features?
How happy are our employees today?
explanation: Unrealized Value asks whether more value can be created in this or other markets and whether pursuing it is worth the effort and risk.

stem: A regulator sets a deadline for a compliance change. How does this affect ordering?
options: Developers fit it in when capacity allows
Deadline and penalty risk raise its order
It goes in a separate compliance backlog
It is ordered like any other feature
explanation: Risk and deadlines are part of value. Missing a legal deadline can cost far more than a delayed feature, so the Product Owner orders the item accordingly.

stem: Which ordering technique does Scrum require?
explanation: Scrum does not prescribe any ordering technique. The Product Owner may use whichever helps maximize value.

stem: A product has many stakeholders. Where do their needs come together?
explanation: The Product Owner represents the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog and orders them into one view of what matters most.

stem: A cumulative flow diagram mainly helps a team see:
options: How work moves through each stage
How much work remains this Sprint
How total scope grows over time
explanation: A cumulative flow diagram shows how much work sits in each stage over time, revealing bottlenecks and flow. It is one of the forecasting practices the Scrum Guide mentions.

stem: The Product Owner often misses the Sprint Retrospective. Why does this matter?
options: The Sprint Goal is not reviewed
The Product Backlog is not refined
explanation: The Retrospective inspects how the last Sprint went for individuals, interactions, processes and tools. Many issues, such as unclear items, involve the Product Owner.

stem: A stakeholder asks why the product exists at all. Which artifact or tool answers best?
explanation: The Product Vision states the purpose of the product, the value it should deliver and to whom.

stem: What does the Product Cost Ratio compare?
options: Effort on new features against total effort
Revenue against the number of employees
explanation: The Product Cost Ratio compares total expenses and costs for the product, operational costs included, with the revenue it brings.

stem: Refinement keeps raising the same unanswered question about an item. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Get the answer from users or stakeholders
Add it to the Sprint and clarify it there
Ask the Developers to agree an assumption
Leave it for the Developers to settle mid-Sprint
explanation: The Product Owner creates and clearly communicates items. Getting the missing information keeps the item ready to be Done when selected.

stem: A stakeholder goes around the Product Owner and asks the Scrum Master to add work to the Sprint. What should happen?
options: Scrum Master raises it at the Daily Scrum
Redirect them to the Product Owner
Developers add it if the Sprint Goal allows
Scrum Master adds it to the next Sprint
explanation: Requests go to the Product Owner, who orders the Product Backlog. The Scrum Master helps the organization respect that and removes the barrier.

stem: True or false: Burn-downs and burn-ups replace the need for empiricism.
explanation: The Scrum Guide says these practices are useful but do not replace the importance of empiricism.

stem: True or false: The Scrum Guide requires Product Backlog items to be written as user stories.
explanation: Scrum does not prescribe a format for Product Backlog items. User stories are one optional practice a team may choose.

stem: Which is the best example of an Immediate Tactical Goal?
options: Become the market leader in our region by 2030
Improve the sign-up experience for users
Cut sign-up drop-off by 10% this quarter
Ship the redesigned sign-up page this quarter
explanation: Immediate Tactical Goals are near-term, measurable outcomes. Leading the region is a Strategic Goal, and shipping a page is an output, not an outcome customers experience.

stem: What does the On-Product Index show?
options: Share of effort spent on new capabilities
Usage of each feature by customers
Share of time teams spend on product work
explanation: The On-Product Index is the percentage of time teams spend working on product and value, rather than other demands.

stem: True or false: Developers may build work a stakeholder asks for directly, outside the Product Backlog.
explanation: The Product Backlog is the single source of work. Requests go through the Product Owner, who orders them with everything else.

stem: True or false: Stakeholders at the Sprint Review can influence the Product Backlog.
explanation: During the Sprint Review the Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet new opportunities, using what attendees learn and discuss.

stem: A product must ship for a trade show. Which approach best protects value?
options: Order by value and release what is Done
Relax the Definition of Done near the end
Lock scope early and plan backwards
Add Developers in the final Sprints
explanation: With a fixed date, ordering by value ensures the most important items are Done. Skipping testing or freezing learning puts value at risk.

stem: Which question does the Product Owner mainly help answer in Sprint Planning?
options: How will the work get done?
How much work can be done?
explanation: The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility this Sprint. The 'how' belongs to the Developers.

stem: True or false: Without an effective Mission and Vision, goals lack a compelling purpose.
explanation: The EBM Guide says that without effective Mission and Vision statements, goals lack a compelling purpose, especially when people work under uncertainty.

stem: True or false: Scrum.org describes the value of a product as measurable.
explanation: Scrum.org's competency description says a product has a clear goal, stakeholders and users, and that the value of the product is measurable.

stem: A low-value item is cheap and blocks nothing. Should it go to the top because it is quick?
options: No; cheap items go to the bottom
Yes, if the Developers have spare capacity
Yes, if it clears clutter from the backlog
explanation: Cost matters, but a quick item with little value does not jump the queue for that reason alone. The Product Owner weighs value against cost and risk.

stem: Customers ask for a 'faster horse'. What should the Product Owner focus on?
explanation: Requests often describe a solution. Understanding the underlying need lets the team find the most valuable way to meet it.

stem: Customer cycle time measures what?
options: Start of release work to actual release
Bug report to the fix being live
Idea to learning from users' use of it
explanation: Customer cycle time is the time from when work starts on a release until it is actually released. It is a Time-to-Market measure.

stem: How do people outside the Scrum Team change the Product Backlog?
options: By agreeing it with the Scrum Master
By raising it at the Sprint Retrospective
By adding it through a change request
explanation: The Scrum Guide says those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

stem: A Product Owner wants to cut uncertainty about a new market. Which two Scrum practices help most? (Choose two.)
options: Delivering a usable Increment every Sprint
Writing a detailed market requirements file
Fixing the Product Backlog for a quarter
Running a longer first Sprint to plan well
explanation: Frequent usable Increments and regular inspection with stakeholders give evidence that reduces uncertainty. Up-front detail and frozen backlogs delay that learning.

stem: Product teams deliver Increments, but leaders never review strategy against the results. What is lost?
options: Clarity of each team's Sprint Goal
Chance to adapt strategy to evidence
Funding for the next round of work
explanation: Business strategy should be inspected and adapted using feedback from product Increments. Ignoring the results wastes that evidence.

stem: Release stabilization period measures the time spent on what?
options: Time from an idea to user learning
Time to restore a failed service
Fixes after work is declared ready
explanation: Release stabilization period is the time spent correcting product problems between the point the developers say it is ready to release and the actual release. It is a Time-to-Market measure.

stem: A stakeholder expects a feature in two weeks that is low in the backlog. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Explain the order and give a forecast
Move it up to keep the stakeholder's trust
Promise a date once it is refined
Escalate to the sponsor to settle the date
explanation: Honest, transparent communication about order and forecasts manages expectations. Promises that ignore the backlog erode trust.

stem: Why give stakeholders a range rather than one date?
options: It avoids having to update it
It leaves room for extra scope
explanation: A range communicates how certain the forecast is. A single date suggests more certainty than complex work allows.

stem: Which two are sound reasons to move an item up the Product Backlog? (Choose two.)
options: It has been waiting the longest
Its requester sits on the steering group
It is the easiest item to estimate
explanation: Risk and dependencies are good reasons to order an item higher. Author, age and description length say nothing about value.

stem: The Product Owner wants a feature by a trade show and asks the Developers to work weekends. What fits Scrum best?
options: Release with known defects, fix later
Add Developers for the last two Sprints
Adjust scope with them, keeping quality
Agree overtime only for the final Sprint
explanation: The Product Owner manages value by choosing what to build, not by pushing effort. Working with the Developers on scope keeps quality and the Definition of Done intact.

stem: A Product Owner is asked to drop the vision because 'the backlog is enough'. What is the best answer?
options: The vision fixes scope; the backlog adds detail
The vision is for sponsors; the backlog for teams
The vision sets the order; the backlog the size
The vision explains why; the backlog lists what
explanation: The Product Vision expresses the purpose and value of the product, which guides ordering. The Product Backlog lists what is needed to improve the product.

stem: Which question belongs to Current Value?
options: How happy are users and customers today?
Can we create value in other markets too?
What stops us delivering new value?
How fast can we test new ideas?
explanation: Current Value asks how happy users, customers, employees and investors are today. The others belong to Unrealized Value, Time-to-Market and Ability to Innovate.

stem: Survey answers say users want feature X, but usage data shows they rarely use similar features. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Trust the usage data and drop X
Test X cheaply before building it all
Order X by the value users stated
Build X, as users asked for it directly
explanation: When signals conflict, a small experiment gives evidence before a large investment. Both the survey and the data are inputs, not proof.

stem: Releases need two weeks of manual sign-off after each Increment is Done. What is the Product Owner's main concern?
options: Increments pile up in the Sprint Backlog
Developers lose time set aside for learning
Users wait longer and learning slows
Testers become a bottleneck for the team
explanation: Slow release processes stretch Time-to-Market, so users get value and the team gets feedback later. Making the delay transparent helps remove it.

stem: What makes an item small enough for Sprint Planning?
options: It has been estimated in story points
It fits in one Developer's week
It can be Done within one Sprint
explanation: Items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning.

stem: Which two are the Product Owner's decisions? (Choose two.)
options: How much work fits the Sprint
explanation: The Product Owner develops and communicates the Product Goal and orders the Product Backlog. How work is built, who does it and how the Daily Scrum runs belong to the Developers.

stem: According to the EBM Guide, beliefs about what is valuable stay assumptions until when?
explanation: The EBM Guide says beliefs in what is valuable are merely assumptions until they are validated by customers.

stem: A Product Owner can fund one of two new ideas. Both sound promising. What is the best first move?
options: Pick the one with the stronger business case
Run a small experiment to test each idea
Ask key customers which they prefer
Fund the idea senior stakeholders back, then measure uptake
explanation: Without evidence both ideas are assumptions. A small experiment tests the hypothesis cheaply before larger investment, as EBM recommends.

stem: Which two are signs of healthy stakeholder collaboration? (Choose two.)
explanation: Healthy collaboration means stakeholders inspect Increments and their feedback adapts the Product Backlog. Task assignment and the Daily Scrum belong to the Developers.

stem: Which two make a release forecast more reliable? (Choose two.)
options: Adding a fixed buffer of 20 percent
Updating it as new data arrives
explanation: Forecasts based on real progress and revised as evidence arrives stay realistic. Fixed first estimates, wished-for dates and started work mislead.

stem: An item has sat untouched at the bottom for two years. What is often the right move?
options: Raise its order so it finally gets done
Move it to an archive section of the backlog
Consider removing it from the backlog
Refine it so it is ready if needed
explanation: Old items that no longer serve the Product Goal add noise. Removing them keeps the Product Backlog transparent and easier to order.
